name: Sundiata Keita
info: Sundiata Keita (c. 1217 – c. 1255) was a Mandinka prince who defeated Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at Kirina and founded the Mali Empire, remembered above all through the Epic of Sundiata kept by the griots.

facts.born: c. 1217; son of Naré Maghann Konaté, king of the Mandinka, and Sogolon Condé, according to the oral tradition
facts.died: c. 1255; the generally accepted account is that he drowned in the Sankarani River near Niani, though other versions exist
facts.role: Prince of the Mandinka; first Mansa (emperor) of the Mali Empire from his victory at Kirina, c. 1235
facts.known: Founding the Mali Empire; victory over Soumaoro Kanté at the Battle of Kirina; the Epic of Sundiata; the Kouroukan Fouga or Manden Charter; first ruler to take the title Mansa; capital at Niani

t: Sundiata Keita defeated King Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at the Battle of Kirina, c. 1235, and became the first Mansa of the Mali Empire.
Most of what is told of his life comes from the Epic of Sundiata, an oral tradition of the Maninka griots, while Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun, writing a century later, confirm that he existed.
The social and political norms of Mali, the Gbara and the Kouroukan Fouga, were first being codified in his reign, and the Manden Charter is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
dyk: The name Sundiata praises him through his mother: it means "the lion of Sogolon", from Sogolon and Jata, lion.
ev: Sundiata is born, son of Naré Maghann Konaté and Sogolon Condé
Sundiata and his allies defeat King Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at the Battle of Kirina
He becomes the first Mansa of the Mali Empire and sets his capital at Niani
His general Tiramakhan Traore defeats the king of Jolof and conquers the Senegambia and Kaabu
Sundiata dies, by the generally accepted account drowned in the Sankarani River

sections.early:
Sundiata Keita was born around 1217. According to the oral traditions passed down by the griots (djeli or jeliw), he was the son of Naré Maghann Konaté, a Mandinka king, and Sogolon Condé, called the daughter of the "buffalo woman". The tradition tells that Sundiata was crippled from childhood and that his mother was ridiculed by her co-wives for her son's disability. Determined to walk like his peers, he one day got up and walked, the epic says miraculously, and became a leader among them.

His paternal half-brother, Dankaran Touman, and Dankaran's mother, Sassouma Bereté, are remembered as cruel and resentful of Sundiata and his mother, and their cruelty grew after the death of Naré Maghann. To escape threats on her son's life, Sogolon took her children into exile, which by the tradition lasted many years and led through lands of the Ghana Empire to Mema, whose king gave them asylum and admired Sundiata for his courage, granting him a senior position. The Mandinka epic gives no dates; the dates and a genealogy come from Arab and North African writers who visited the region about a century later.
sections.rise:
When King Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso conquered the Mandinka, messengers, by the tradition, went to look for Sogolon and her children, since a prophecy held that Sundiata would be a great leader. They found him in Mema and persuaded him to return and free the Mandinka. He came back with an army given to him by the king of Mema. On the plain of Siby he and the warlords of his age group, among them Tabon Wana, Kamadia Kamara, Faony Condé, Siara Kuman Konaté and Tiramakhan Traore, formed a pact of brotherhood against the Sosso king.

The consensus is that in c. 1235 Sundiata, who had survived one of Soumaoro's earlier raids, went to war with his allies and defeated Soumaoro at the Battle of Kirina. He became the first emperor of the Mali Empire and the first of the Mandinka line of kings to take the royal title Mansa, king or emperor in Mandinka. The French ethnographer Maurice Delafosse had proposed a fuller story of the Sosso kings, including a father named Diara Kanté, but his account has been refuted by scholars such as Monteil and Cornevin, and no Diara Kanté appears in the oral sources.
sections.deeds:
After Kirina, Sundiata took control of the states the Sosso had conquered and gave privileges to those who had fought against Soumaoro. He set his capital at Niani, near the present-day border between Mali and Guinea. With his generals, of whom Tiramakhan Traore was among the most prominent, he went on to conquer other states, including the lands of the old Ghana Empire; Sundiata himself is credited with the conquest of Diafunu and Kita. Tiramakhan defeated the king of Jolof and made his kingdom a vassal, then went deep into present-day Senegal, the Gambia and Guinea-Bissau; in Kaabu he defeated and killed the last great Bainuk king, Kikikor, and annexed his state.

Sundiata was not an absolute monarch, whatever his title implies. The empire was reportedly run like a federation, each clan, first the Mandinka clans of Traore, Kamara, Koroma, Konde and Keita, having a chief representative at court, and the Great Gbara Assembly checked the Mansa's power, enforced his edicts and chose his successor. He controlled the region's trade routes and gold fields, and is reported to have developed agriculture and introduced cotton and weaving in Mali.
sections.opponents:
Sundiata's great enemy was Soumaoro Kanté, king of Sosso, whom the traditions remember as a valiant warrior and as one of the true champions of the traditional African religion; according to Fyle, Soumaoro invented the balafon and the dan, a four-string guitar of hunters and griots. Soumaoro's allies were defeated after Kirina, in particular the king of Jolof. Serer oral tradition tells of "the robbery of the horses": when Sundiata sent men with gold to buy horses in Jolof, the king took both gold and horses, and Sundiata sent his general to kill him. Djibril Tamsir Niane wrote that the Jolof king sided with Soumaoro because, like him, he was hostile to Islam.

Sundiata's own religion is disputed. Niane alludes to his being a Muslim, but according to Fage nothing in the original epic supports this; he is remembered as a great hunter and magician whose subjects, like him, mostly held traditional beliefs. Some Muslim griots later added that he descended from companions of Muhammad and was a successor of Dhu al-Qarnayn, claims that G. Wesley Johnson calls a search for "Islamic legitimacy".
sections.last:
The generally accepted year of Sundiata's death is c. 1255, but little is known of how he died, and the versions, mostly modern, differ. Mandinka tradition also forbids revealing the burial places of its great kings. According to some he drowned while trying to cross the Sankarani River near Niani. Delafosse wrote that he was "accidentally killed by an arrow during a ceremony", and others have held that he was assassinated at a public demonstration known as a Gitten.

The account now generally accepted is drowning in the Sankarani River near his capital, where a shrine bearing his name, Sundiata-dun, "Sundiata's deep water", still stands. His three sons, Mansa Wali Keita, Mansa Ouati Keita and Mansa Khalifa Keita, succeeded him as Mansas of the empire, and the famously ostentatious Mansa Musa was later to rule as his great-nephew. Towards the end of his reign, "absolute security" is reported to have "prevailed throughout his dominion". The empire he founded flourished from the 13th to the late 14th century, until vassal states threw off Mali's rule, some of them founding empires of their own.
sections.legacy:
Under Sundiata Mali first began to become an economic power, a trend his successors continued; Mansa Musa, the famously wealthy ruler of the next century, was his great-nephew. Credit for Mali's conquests is shared with his generals, Tiramakhan Traore above all, but he is remembered as a leader who commanded the loyalty of his generals and army. The Gbara and the Kouroukan Fouga, the social and political constitution first codified in his reign, were never written down at the time and changed in the retelling, yet many of their laws have been incorporated into the constitution of modern Mali, and UNESCO lists the Manden Charter as intangible cultural heritage.

He lives above all in the Epic of Sundiata, the semi-historical, legendary poem of the Malinké that griots have handed down for generations, which shows the influence of what Ralph Austen calls "Islamicate" culture. Scholars disagree even over his surname: some propose that Keita is a royal or clan name meaning heir, and that his family name was Konaté. The epic is taught far beyond West Africa; Mary Ellen Snodgrass and others have noted its likeness to Disney's The Lion King, which Disney says drew on Hamlet.

summary: Sundiata Keita defeated Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at Kirina around 1235 and became the first Mansa of the Mali Empire, ruling from Niani with a council of clans and generals such as Tiramakhan Traore. Known chiefly through the griots' Epic of Sundiata, he died around 1255, by the accepted account drowned in the Sankarani River.

notes: The article is short (about 3,300 words); several sections are thin and lean on the oral tradition, which is marked as such.
Dates of birth and death are both c. as the article gives them; the c. 1235 Battle of Kirina is 'the consensus'.
No date in the article for Tiramakhan's conquests; given as '13th century' in the events.
Left out: the claim that Mansa Musa is the wealthiest person of all time (the article itself doubts it can be calculated); the video-game mentions.
Ibn Battuta's 'Sariq Jata' grandfather claim left out as the article judges it mistaken genealogy.
